vignette: Mang Dado, 71, has hypertension and is 36 hours after an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere. He has weakness of the right arm and leg, trouble finding words although he follows simple commands, and cannot see to his right with either eye. His blood pressure is 178/96 and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. At lunch, his tray is placed on his right side. He bumps the tray with his right hand, coughs repeatedly when his son gives him a sip of water, and his voice sounds wet afterward. The son wants him to eat now so that he can regain strength.
stem: What should the nurse do first?
options: Offer thickened liquids in small amounts with him upright
Move the tray to his left side and let him feed himself
Hold oral intake and request a swallowing evaluation
Encourage the son to give soft foods one spoon at a time
optionRationales: Right action, wrong time: texture changes are used only after a swallow assessment.
Right detail for hemianopsia but does not address the aspiration sign.
Right: protects the airway until swallowing is judged safe.
Unsafe but common habit: family feeding before evaluation increases risk.
rationale:
1. Coughing with sips and a wet voice after swallowing are signs of aspiration, a threat to the airway.
2. Priority rule: airway and breathing before nutrition, so oral intake is held until a swallowing screen is done.
3. Positioning and food choices are used only after the swallow is judged safe.
Flip: if he swallowed water without coughing or voice change, feeding with upright positioning would be appropriate.
strategy: Safety: protect the airway before feeding
keyFacts: Check gag reflex and swallow before feeding
Aspiration risk signs: cough, wet voice

vignette: Mang Dado, 71, has hypertension and is 36 hours after an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere. He has weakness of the right arm and leg, trouble finding words although he follows simple commands, and cannot see to his right with either eye. His blood pressure is 178/96 and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. At lunch, his tray is placed on his right side. He bumps the tray with his right hand, coughs repeatedly when his son gives him a sip of water, and his voice sounds wet afterward. The son wants him to eat now so that he can regain strength.
stem: Where should the nurse place the tray and the call light, and from which side should the nurse approach?
options: On the right side so that he practises using that arm
On the left side, approaching from the left
In the center of the table, approaching from the foot of the bed
On the right side, approaching quietly from behind
optionRationales: Right action for rehabilitation but unsafe when he cannot see the right side.
Right: matches his intact visual field.
Plausible but not matched to the field defect.
Unsafe: approaching from the blind side startles him.
rationale: He cannot see the right half of the visual field, so objects and people must be on the left side where he can see them. He should also be taught to turn his head toward the right to scan.
keyFacts: Place items on the unaffected, seeing side
Teach scanning to the blind side

vignette: Mang Dado, 71, has hypertension and is 36 hours after an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere. He has weakness of the right arm and leg, trouble finding words although he follows simple commands, and cannot see to his right with either eye. His blood pressure is 178/96 and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. At lunch, his tray is placed on his right side. He bumps the tray with his right hand, coughs repeatedly when his son gives him a sip of water, and his voice sounds wet afterward. The son wants him to eat now so that he can regain strength.
stem: Match each deficit with the most appropriate nursing action.
rows: Wet voice after sips of water
columns: Teach him to turn his head to scan
rationale: Visual field loss needs scanning teaching. Aphasia needs short phrases with gestures and time. Dysphagia needs a swallow check before feeding. Weakness needs range of motion and alignment.
optionRationales: Right (teach him to scan): with right visual field loss he must turn his head to see the right side. Speech or swallow measures do not help vision.
Right (short phrases with gestures): difficulty finding words is aphasia, so use short phrases, gestures and time. Do not shout or talk fast.
Right (hold intake until swallow check): a wet voice after sips signals aspiration risk, so nothing by mouth until the swallow screen is done. Airway safety comes first.
Right (range of motion and alignment): a weak arm needs positioning and range of motion to prevent contracture and shoulder injury. It does not affect swallowing or vision.
keyFacts: Aphasia: short sentences, gestures
Hemiparesis: ROM and alignment

vignette: Mang Dado, 71, has hypertension and is 36 hours after an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere. He has weakness of the right arm and leg, trouble finding words although he follows simple commands, and cannot see to his right with either eye. His blood pressure is 178/96 and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. At lunch, his tray is placed on his right side. He bumps the tray with his right hand, coughs repeatedly when his son gives him a sip of water, and his voice sounds wet afterward. The son wants him to eat now so that he can regain strength.
stem: A stroke in the left hemisphere causes {{1}}-sided weakness and commonly {{2}}.
rationale: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, and speech is dominated by the left hemisphere in most people, so left strokes cause right weakness and aphasia.
optionRationales: Right: the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body, so a left stroke causes right-sided weakness. Left-sided weakness would come from a right stroke.
Right: language is controlled by the left hemisphere in most people, so aphasia is common. Neglect of the left side and impulsive behavior come from right-sided strokes. Hearing loss is not typical.
keyFacts: Left stroke: right weakness, aphasia

vignette: Mang Dado, 71, has hypertension and is 36 hours after an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere. He has weakness of the right arm and leg, trouble finding words although he follows simple commands, and cannot see to his right with either eye. His blood pressure is 178/96 and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. At lunch, his tray is placed on his right side. He bumps the tray with his right hand, coughs repeatedly when his son gives him a sip of water, and his voice sounds wet afterward. The son wants him to eat now so that he can regain strength.
stem: Select the findings that show he is at risk of aspiration.
options: Coughs repeatedly after a sip of water
Voice sounds wet afterward
Weakness of the right arm
Blood pressure 178/96
Son wants him to eat now
Glasgow Coma Scale score 14
optionRationales: Aspiration risk: coughing after a sip shows liquid is entering the airway.
Aspiration risk: a wet voice after swallowing suggests liquid remains near the airway.
Not an aspiration sign: arm weakness is a motor deficit and does not show unsafe swallowing.
Not an aspiration cue.
Pressure to feed, not a finding.
Alertness is adequate.
rationale: Coughing after sips and a wet voice are signs of unsafe swallowing. Weakness, blood pressure and the son's wish are not aspiration cues.
keyFacts: Cough and wet voice after swallowing

vignette: Aling Cora, 72, is on postoperative day 1 after a right total hip replacement for osteoarthritis. An abduction wedge pillow is between her legs and she is receiving pain medication through a patient-controlled device. At 0800 she turns toward her bedside table to reach her glasses and suddenly cries out with sharp pain in her right hip. Her right leg now looks shorter than the left and lies in an unusual position. Her temperature is 37.2 C and her pedal pulses are present. Her daughter asks if she can sit in the soft low armchair by the bed for breakfast.
stem: What should the nurse do first?
options: Help her stand to see if the pain eases with weight-bearing
Apply ice to the hip and give the next patient-controlled dose
Gently move the leg back into abduction on the wedge pillow
Keep the leg still and notify the surgeon immediately
optionRationales: Unsafe: weight-bearing on a dislocated joint causes damage.
Treats the symptom: comfort measures do not address dislocation.
Over-intervention: reducing a dislocation is not a nursing action.
Right: immobilise and report.
rationale:
1. Sudden severe pain with a shortened, abnormally positioned leg after a movement is the pattern of a prosthesis dislocation.
2. The nurse keeps the limb immobile and still, and notifies the surgeon at once; moving the leg risks nerve and vessel injury.
3. Ice and ambulation are not first actions.
Flip: if the pain were mild and the leg properly aligned, repositioning with pillows and rechecking would come first.
strategy: Immobilise and report: do not manipulate
keyFacts: Dislocation: sudden pain, shortened, abnormal position
Do not try to reposition

vignette: Aling Cora, 72, is on postoperative day 1 after a right total hip replacement for osteoarthritis. An abduction wedge pillow is between her legs and she is receiving pain medication through a patient-controlled device. At 0800 she turns toward her bedside table to reach her glasses and suddenly cries out with sharp pain in her right hip. Her right leg now looks shorter than the left and lies in an unusual position. Her temperature is 37.2 C and her pedal pulses are present. Her daughter asks if she can sit in the soft low armchair by the bed for breakfast.
stem: Which statement by Aling Cora, later, shows she understands hip precautions?
options: I will cross my legs at the knees when I sit
I will bend forward to put on my own shoes
I will rest in my soft low armchair
I will use a raised toilet seat and a high chair
optionRationales: Unsafe: crossing legs adducts the hip.
Unsafe: bending forward flexes the hip beyond 90 degrees.
Unsafe: low seats flex the hip.
Right: keeps flexion under 90 degrees.
rationale: Raised toilet seats and high chairs keep the hip above 90 degrees of flexion. Low soft chairs, crossing legs and bending forward to reach her feet flex the hip and risk dislocation.
keyFacts: Never flex the hip beyond 90 degrees
Use high seats and raised toilet seat

vignette: Aling Cora, 72, is on postoperative day 1 after a right total hip replacement for osteoarthritis. An abduction wedge pillow is between her legs and she is receiving pain medication through a patient-controlled device. At 0800 she turns toward her bedside table to reach her glasses and suddenly cries out with sharp pain in her right hip. Her right leg now looks shorter than the left and lies in an unusual position. Her temperature is 37.2 C and her pedal pulses are present. Her daughter asks if she can sit in the soft low armchair by the bed for breakfast.
stem: Classify each activity as safe or unsafe after the hip replacement.
rows: Sitting in a low soft chair
Crossing the legs at the knees
Sleeping with a pillow between the knees
rationale: A pillow between the legs keeps abduction. Raised seats keep flexion under 90 degrees. Low soft chairs and crossing the legs risk dislocation.
optionRationales: Right (unsafe): a low soft chair makes the hip flex beyond 90 degrees, risking dislocation. Use a firm, raised seat.
Right (safe): a raised toilet seat keeps hip flexion below 90 degrees, so it protects the new joint.
Right (unsafe): crossing the legs brings the leg across the midline (adduction), which can dislocate the hip.
Right (safe): a pillow between the knees keeps the legs apart (abduction), which protects the new joint.
keyFacts: Keep abduction, avoid adduction and over-flexion

vignette: Aling Cora, 72, is on postoperative day 1 after a right total hip replacement for osteoarthritis. An abduction wedge pillow is between her legs and she is receiving pain medication through a patient-controlled device. At 0800 she turns toward her bedside table to reach her glasses and suddenly cries out with sharp pain in her right hip. Her right leg now looks shorter than the left and lies in an unusual position. Her temperature is 37.2 C and her pedal pulses are present. Her daughter asks if she can sit in the soft low armchair by the bed for breakfast.
stem: The nurse must never flex the hip beyond {{1}} degrees and keeps the leg in {{2}}.
rationale: The femoral head stays seated when flexion stays within 90 degrees and the leg is kept abducted.
optionRationales: Right: hip flexion beyond 90 degrees can dislocate the joint after replacement. 45 is too low to be the limit, while 120 and 135 are unsafe.
Right: abduction keeps the head of the femur seated. Adduction and internal rotation are the movements that cause dislocation.
keyFacts: Flexion under 90 degrees; abduction

vignette: Aling Cora, 72, is on postoperative day 1 after a right total hip replacement for osteoarthritis. An abduction wedge pillow is between her legs and she is receiving pain medication through a patient-controlled device. At 0800 she turns toward her bedside table to reach her glasses and suddenly cries out with sharp pain in her right hip. Her right leg now looks shorter than the left and lies in an unusual position. Her temperature is 37.2 C and her pedal pulses are present. Her daughter asks if she can sit in the soft low armchair by the bed for breakfast.
stem: Select the findings that suggest the prosthesis has dislocated.
options: Sudden sharp pain after turning
Right leg looks shorter
Leg lies in an unusual position
Temperature 37.2 C
Pedal pulses present
Wedge pillow between the legs
optionRationales: Suggests dislocation: sudden sharp pain after turning suggests the joint has moved out of place.
Suggests dislocation: a shortened leg means the head of the prosthesis has moved out of its socket.
Suggests dislocation: an unusual leg position, often turned inward or outward, suggests the joint is out of place.
Not a sign of dislocation: a temperature of 37.2 C is normal and unrelated.
Not a sign of dislocation: present pedal pulses show circulation is intact and are unrelated.
Not a sign of dislocation: the wedge pillow is a correct precaution that prevents dislocation.
rationale: Sudden sharp pain with movement, a shortened leg and an unusual leg position suggest dislocation. Temperature, pedal pulses, patient-controlled analgesia and the wedge pillow are unrelated.
strategy: Separate dislocation cues from normal data
keyFacts: Dislocation: sudden pain, leg shortening, abnormal position

vignette: Marco, 24, has schizophrenia and was started on a high-potency antipsychotic three days ago on the psychiatric unit. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upward and his tongue feels thick; he is struggling to swallow his saliva. Six days later, after the dose was increased, he has a temperature of 39.6 C, severe muscle rigidity, sweating, a blood pressure that swings between 170/100 and 90/60, and increasing confusion.
stem: On the morning of day 3, what should the nurse do first?
options: Give the next scheduled antipsychotic dose and observe
Reassure him that the stiffness is anxiety and will pass
Assess his airway and call the provider for an anticholinergic order
Document the finding and reassess at the end of the shift
optionRationales: Unsafe: continuing the drug worsens dystonia.
Under-reaction: attributes a drug effect to anxiety.
Right: protects the airway and obtains treatment.
Under-reaction: delays an emergency.
rationale:
1. Neck twisting, upward gaze, thick tongue and trouble swallowing are acute dystonia, which can progress to laryngospasm.
2. Priority is airway and breathing, then an order for an anticholinergic.
3. Reassurance or waiting is unsafe.
Flip: if he had only mild restlessness, the nurse would report it at the next opportunity.
keyFacts: Acute dystonia is an emergency
Treat with anticholinergic

vignette: Marco, 24, has schizophrenia and was started on a high-potency antipsychotic three days ago on the psychiatric unit. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upward and his tongue feels thick; he is struggling to swallow his saliva. Six days later, after the dose was increased, he has a temperature of 39.6 C, severe muscle rigidity, sweating, a blood pressure that swings between 170/100 and 90/60, and increasing confusion.
stem: On day 6, what should the nurse do first?
options: Give the PRN anticholinergic and recheck in an hour
Hold the antipsychotic and notify the provider urgently
Apply cooling blankets and continue the schedule
Reassure him and encourage fluids
optionRationales: Treats the wrong problem: anticholinergics treat EPS, not NMS.
Right: stopping the antipsychotic is the first treatment step.
Treats the symptom: fever without stopping the cause.
Wrong: reassuring him and encouraging fluids under-reacts to a life-threatening reaction that needs the drug held and the provider called.
rationale:
Fever, severe rigidity, unstable blood pressure, sweating and confusion after a dose increase are NMS, a life-threatening reaction. The drug is held and the provider called immediately; cooling and fluids follow.
Flip: if he had rigidity with no fever and stable vital signs, an anticholinergic for pseudoparkinsonism would be reasonable.
keyFacts: NMS: fever, rigidity, unstable BP, confusion; stop the drug

vignette: Marco, 24, has schizophrenia and was started on a high-potency antipsychotic three days ago on the psychiatric unit. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upward and his tongue feels thick; he is struggling to swallow his saliva. Six days later, after the dose was increased, he has a temperature of 39.6 C, severe muscle rigidity, sweating, a blood pressure that swings between 170/100 and 90/60, and increasing confusion.
stem: Match each description with the side effect.
rows: Lip smacking after months of therapy
Neck twisting and upward gaze on day 3
rationale: Pacing and an urge to move is akathisia, shuffling gait with pill-rolling is pseudoparkinsonism, lip smacking and worm-like tongue after months is tardive dyskinesia, and early neck twisting is acute dystonia.
optionRationales: Right (akathisia): restless pacing and being unable to sit still is the picture of akathisia, not a tremor or a muscle spasm.
Right (pseudoparkinsonism): shuffling gait with pill-rolling tremor mimics Parkinson disease and is drug-induced.
Right (tardive dyskinesia): lip smacking and tongue movements after months of therapy are late, often permanent movements. Report them early.
Right (acute dystonia): sudden neck twisting and upward gaze within days is an emergency spasm. It responds to anticholinergic drugs.
keyFacts: EPS types: dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia

vignette: Marco, 24, has schizophrenia and was started on a high-potency antipsychotic three days ago on the psychiatric unit. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upward and his tongue feels thick; he is struggling to swallow his saliva. Six days later, after the dose was increased, he has a temperature of 39.6 C, severe muscle rigidity, sweating, a blood pressure that swings between 170/100 and 90/60, and increasing confusion.
stem: NMS is managed by {{1}} the antipsychotic and giving {{2}}.

choices: supportive care with cooling and hydration
a higher dose of a different antipsychotic

rationale: The causative drug is stopped and the client is cooled and hydrated while the provider manages complications.
optionRationales: Right: the causative antipsychotic must be stopped. Continuing or doubling it worsens neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Right: supportive care with cooling and hydration treats the high fever and muscle breakdown. Restricting fluids harms the kidneys, and another antipsychotic dose repeats the cause.
keyFacts: Stop the drug; cool and hydrate

vignette: Marco, 24, has schizophrenia and was started on a high-potency antipsychotic three days ago on the psychiatric unit. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upward and his tongue feels thick; he is struggling to swallow his saliva. Six days later, after the dose was increased, he has a temperature of 39.6 C, severe muscle rigidity, sweating, a blood pressure that swings between 170/100 and 90/60, and increasing confusion.
stem: Select the findings on day 6 that point to NMS rather than simple EPS.
options: Temperature 39.6 C
Severe muscle rigidity
Blood pressure swings
Increasing confusion
Neck twisted to one side on day 3
Thick tongue on day 3
optionRationales: Points to NMS: a temperature of 39.6 C is a whole-body feature, not seen with simple EPS.
Points to NMS: severe muscle rigidity is a hallmark of NMS, whereas EPS stiffness is milder.
Autonomic instability.
Altered mental state.
Not for NMS: a twisted neck on day 3 was dystonia, an earlier EPS effect.
Not for NMS: a thick tongue on day 3 was dystonia, an earlier EPS effect.
rationale: High fever, severe rigidity, unstable blood pressure and confusion are systemic features of NMS. The earlier neck twisting and thick tongue are dystonia from day 3.
strategy: Systemic signs separate NMS from EPS
keyFacts: NMS has systemic signs; EPS is movement only

vignette: Mang Ben, 38, was rescued from a burning house after being trapped in a closed room. He is anxious and coughing. His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is soot around his mouth. Burns cover the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the whole of his left arm. His respiratory rate is 28/min, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100/60 and the pulse oximeter reads 99% on room air. Bystanders poured water over his burns.
stem: Which action is the priority for the emergency room nurse?
options: Begin fluid resuscitation because the saturation is normal
Cover the burns with clean dry dressings
Give pain medication so that he can breathe comfortably
Give high-flow oxygen and request urgent airway evaluation
optionRationales: Right action, wrong priority: fluids matter, but the airway can fail first.
Right care, wrong time: wounds come after airway and breathing.
Treats the symptom: sedating pain relief can worsen airway risk.
Right: oxygen and early airway control.
rationale:
1. A hoarse voice, singed nasal hair, soot and a closed-space fire suggest inhalation injury, and airway swelling can close the airway within hours.
2. Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so 99% is not reassuring.
3. Give 100% oxygen and request early airway assessment before fluids or wound care.
Flip: if there were no airway cues and burns only on the arm, cooling and fluids would lead.
strategy: Airway first; do not trust the saturation
keyFacts: Airway first
Pulse oximetry may be falsely normal with carbon monoxide

vignette: Mang Ben, 38, was rescued from a burning house after being trapped in a closed room. He is anxious and coughing. His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is soot around his mouth. Burns cover the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the whole of his left arm. His respiratory rate is 28/min, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100/60 and the pulse oximeter reads 99% on room air. Bystanders poured water over his burns.
stem: Using the rule of nines, which estimate of the body surface area burned is most accurate?
optionRationales: Counts the trunk only.
Right: the front of the trunk is 18% and one entire arm is 9%, which add to 27%.
Counts both arms or both sides of the trunk.
Wrong: 45% overestimates the burn and does not match the areas described.
rationale: In an adult the front of the trunk is 18% and one entire arm is 9%, giving 27%.
keyFacts: Rule of nines: front trunk 18%, each arm 9%

vignette: Mang Ben, 38, was rescued from a burning house after being trapped in a closed room. He is anxious and coughing. His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is soot around his mouth. Burns cover the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the whole of his left arm. His respiratory rate is 28/min, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100/60 and the pulse oximeter reads 99% on room air. Bystanders poured water over his burns.
stem: Match each description with the burn depth.
rationale: Superficial burns are red, dry and painful; partial-thickness burns blister and are very painful; full-thickness burns are leathery or charred and painless because the nerve endings are destroyed.
optionRationales: Right (superficial): red, dry and painful with no blisters involves only the top layer. Blistering would mean partial thickness.
Right (partial thickness): blisters, weeping and severe pain mean the deeper layer is injured but nerve endings still work.
Right (full thickness): white or leathery skin without pain means nerve endings are destroyed. A painless burn is more serious, not less.
keyFacts: Full-thickness: painless, leathery

vignette: Mang Ben, 38, was rescued from a burning house after being trapped in a closed room. He is anxious and coughing. His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is soot around his mouth. Burns cover the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the whole of his left arm. His respiratory rate is 28/min, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100/60 and the pulse oximeter reads 99% on room air. Bystanders poured water over his burns.
stem: The fluid rate in the first hours is based on the {{1}} burned and the client's weight, and adequacy is judged by {{2}}.
rationale: Fluid formulas use burn size and weight, and urine output is the key bedside indicator of adequate resuscitation.
optionRationales: Right: burn fluid formulas use the percentage of body surface area burned and weight. Dressings and time since rescue alone do not set the volume.
Right: urine output is the bedside sign of adequate fluid resuscitation. Skin color alone is unreliable and oral intake is not used in a major burn.
keyFacts: Urine output guides fluid adequacy

vignette: Mang Ben, 38, was rescued from a burning house after being trapped in a closed room. He is anxious and coughing. His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is soot around his mouth. Burns cover the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the whole of his left arm. His respiratory rate is 28/min, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100/60 and the pulse oximeter reads 99% on room air. Bystanders poured water over his burns.
stem: Select the findings that suggest an inhalation injury.
options: Hoarse voice
Singed nasal hairs
Soot around the mouth
Trapped in a closed room
Burn on the left arm
Pulse oximeter 99%
optionRationales: Suggests inhalation injury: a hoarse voice shows the airway is swelling.
Suggests inhalation injury: singed nasal hairs show he breathed in hot air.
Suggests inhalation injury: soot around the mouth shows he breathed in smoke.
Suggests inhalation injury: being trapped in a closed room means he breathed smoke in an enclosed space.
Not an airway sign: a burn on the arm does not show injury to the airway.
Can be falsely normal.
rationale: Hoarse voice, singed nasal hairs, soot around the mouth and a closed-space fire are the classic cues. Burns on the arm and a normal oximeter reading do not exclude or define it.
keyFacts: Hoarseness, singed nasal hairs, soot, enclosed space
